item.content:encoded:
The British Council is seeking an International Consultant or Consultancy Firm for the Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) initiative in Sudan, offering an important opportunity for experienced education, skills-development and policy professionals to contribute to the development of a comprehensive national framework designed to recognise skills acquired through formal, non-formal and informal pathways.

The consultancy will provide technical support for the development of a National Recognition of Prior Learning Policy Framework in Sudan, with particular attention to Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET), Non-Formal Education (NFE), higher education, qualifications, assessment, certification, institutional governance and quality assurance.

Applications for the consultancy close on 26 August 2026.

The successful consultant or consultancy firm will be expected to provide technical leadership and work with national stakeholders and development partners to develop a comprehensive, cross-sectoral National RPL Policy Framework that is operational, implementable and ready for government endorsement.

About the British Council International RPL Consultancy in Sudan

The British Council is implementing this initiative through its Youth Skills Programme in Sudan, which is supporting system-level reforms within Technical and Vocational Education and Training and Non-Formal Education.

The broader objective is to improve young people’s access to employment and lifelong learning opportunities.

The need for a Recognition of Prior Learning system is particularly significant within the Sudanese context. Ongoing conflict and displacement mean that a considerable amount of skills acquisition takes place through informal and non-formal channels.

People may develop valuable competencies through work, community activities, informal training, apprenticeships and other experiences without necessarily receiving formal qualifications recognising what they have learned.

When such competencies remain unrecognised by formal education and training systems, individuals can face difficulties progressing into further education or securing employment that appropriately reflects their capabilities.

The British Council initiative therefore seeks to help address the gap between skills acquired outside conventional formal education and the qualifications and recognition available through established systems.

Background to the Recognition of Prior Learning Initiative

The consultancy does not begin from scratch. It builds on earlier policy work and stakeholder engagement concerning Recognition of Prior Learning in Sudan.

In March 2026, the British Council convened a national Policy Dialogue on Recognition of Prior Learning.

The dialogue brought together stakeholders including:

  • Ministry of Education;
  • Ministry of Higher Education;
  • Ministry of Labour;
  • Supreme Council for Vocational Training and Apprenticeship;
  • National Centre for Curriculum and Educational Research;
  • Private-sector representatives;
  • Trade unions;
  • Civil society organisations; and
  • Development partners.

The national dialogue produced two particularly important outputs.

The first was a Policy Brief outlining key principles and system components required for Recognition of Prior Learning.

The second was a Roadmap identifying phased steps for designing and implementing an RPL system.

The Policy Brief identified critical areas such as regulatory frameworks, institutional arrangements, financing, quality assurance and stakeholder engagement. Meanwhile, the Roadmap established a phased pathway covering system design, implementation and continuous improvement.

The new consultancy is intended to build upon these foundations and move the process towards a comprehensive National RPL Policy Framework that can ultimately be considered for government endorsement.

Why the National RPL Framework Is Important for Sudan

Sudan’s political, economic and humanitarian circumstances have placed considerable pressure on the country’s skills system and labour market.

Conflict has disrupted education, contributed to widespread displacement and severely constrained or rendered non-operational parts of the education system.

At the same time, young people represent a substantial proportion of Sudan’s population, while unemployment remains high and the informal economy plays a dominant role.

These circumstances create significant challenges for young people attempting to enter skilled, sustainable employment.

Sectors with potential for economic growth require workers equipped with practical competencies and professional skills. However, disruption to education and limited access to quality learning have increased the importance of developing a skills system that is responsive, inclusive and resilient.

A well-designed Recognition of Prior Learning framework could help create mechanisms through which existing competencies can be assessed, recognised and potentially connected with qualifications, further learning and employment pathways.

Programmes Supporting the Initiative

The activity forms part of the British Council’s Going Global Partnerships (GGP) and Youth Connect programmes in Sudan.

Going Global Partnerships supports mutually beneficial higher education and TVET collaboration between the United Kingdom and other countries. The programme aims to contribute to stronger, more inclusive and globally connected tertiary systems capable of supporting economic and social growth.

Youth Connect, meanwhile, supports young people in developing the skills, confidence, inspiration and connections required to address major challenges including employability, inequality, conflict and climate change.

The RPL consultancy therefore sits within a broader effort to strengthen education, skills development and opportunities for young people.

Purpose of the British Council RPL Consultancy

The British Council intends to appoint an individual consultant or consultancy firm capable of providing technical guidance and support to Sudan’s TVET and Non-Formal Education systems.

A central responsibility will be the development of a National Recognition of Prior Learning Policy Framework aligned with Sudan’s TVET, NFE and higher education systems.

The assignment is expected to ensure that the resulting framework supports both horizontal and vertical mobility between non-formal, technical and academic pathways.

This is important because an effective RPL system should not merely acknowledge previously acquired competencies. It should also help establish pathways through which recognised learning can support progression between different parts of the education, training and qualifications system.

The consultant or firm must consequently work towards an operational and implementable framework covering areas such as:

  • Governance;
  • Assessment;
  • Certification;
  • Quality assurance;
  • Institutional responsibilities;
  • Policy and legal provisions;
  • Qualifications;
  • Mobility between learning pathways; and
  • Practical implementation.

The consultant will also facilitate a co-creation process involving national stakeholders and development partners to strengthen national ownership and prepare the framework for endorsement.

Scope of Work for the International RPL Consultant

The consultancy involves an extensive scope of work covering policy design, institutional governance, assessment, certification, quality assurance, implementation, stakeholder consultation and endorsement support.

1. System Design and Policy Development

The consultant or consultancy firm will begin by reviewing and consolidating the existing RPL Policy Brief and Roadmap.

The assignment will require analysis of Sudan’s existing:

  • Legal landscape;
  • Institutional environment; and
  • Qualifications landscape.

Using this analysis and the existing policy work, the consultant will design a comprehensive National Recognition of Prior Learning Policy Framework.

The framework is expected to address:

  • Policy provisions;
  • Legal provisions;
  • Integration with national qualifications frameworks; and
  • Cross-sectoral articulation involving TVET, Non-Formal Education and higher education.

This component is fundamental because the RPL system must be connected to Sudan’s broader education, training and qualifications architecture rather than operating as an isolated mechanism.

2. Institutional Architecture and Governance

A national RPL system requires clearly defined institutional responsibilities.

The consultant will therefore define the roles and responsibilities of relevant institutions and stakeholder groups, including:

  • Ministry of Education;
  • Ministry of Higher Education;
  • Ministry of Labour;
  • Supreme Council for Vocational Training and Apprenticeship;
  • National Centre for Curriculum and Educational Research;
  • Training providers;
  • Employers; and
  • Civil society organisations.

The consultant will also propose an appropriate national governance model.

This is expected to cover matters including:

  • Coordination mechanisms;
  • Oversight structures;
  • Implementation responsibilities; and
  • Institutional arrangements required for effective administration of the RPL system.

Recommendations may also involve establishing new RPL units or mechanisms or strengthening existing institutional structures where appropriate.

3. Competency-Based Assessment and Certification Model

Another major component of the consultancy concerns the way people’s existing competencies will actually be assessed and formally recognised.

The consultant will develop a competency-based RPL assessment framework.

Potential assessment methodologies specifically identified within the assignment include:

  • Portfolios;
  • Practical tests; and
  • Interviews.

The framework must also address certification pathways and equivalency mechanisms.

Additionally, the consultant will consider credit transfer and articulation systems, helping establish how recognised competencies could contribute towards qualifications or progression between different education and training pathways.

4. National RPL Quality Assurance Framework

Recognition will only have meaningful long-term value if institutions, employers, learners and other stakeholders can have confidence in the quality and consistency of the system.

The consultant will therefore design a national quality assurance system for RPL.

This will include:

  • National standards;
  • Guidelines;
  • Accreditation mechanisms;
  • Monitoring arrangements;
  • Evaluation processes; and
  • Continuous improvement mechanisms.

The quality assurance framework will be important in supporting consistency, credibility and sustainability across the wider RPL system.

5. RPL Implementation Guidelines and Operational Manual

The assignment extends beyond high-level policy development.

The British Council requires a framework capable of being implemented in practice. The consultant will therefore develop a detailed Operational Manual.

The manual is expected to provide guidance concerning:

  1. Step-by-step implementation processes;
  2. Institutional workflows;
  3. Roles and responsibilities of assessors;
  4. Roles and responsibilities of institutions; and
  5. Learner support mechanisms.

Learner support is expected to include areas such as:

  • Guidance;
  • Counselling; and
  • Bridging mechanisms.

This operational dimension is particularly important because it translates national policy into procedures that institutions and practitioners can actually follow.

6. Stakeholder Engagement and Co-Creation

Stakeholder participation is a central component of the assignment.

The consultant or consultancy firm will facilitate a structured consultation process involving a broad range of stakeholders.

Government stakeholders are expected to include the relevant bodies responsible for education, higher education, labour, vocational training and curriculum development.

Consultations will also involve:

  • Private-sector organisations;
  • Employers;
  • Civil society organisations;
  • Training providers; and
  • Development partners.

Development partners specifically identified in the Terms of Reference include organisations such as:

  • International Labour Organization;
  • UNESCO;
  • Norwegian Refugee Council; and
  • International Organization for Migration.

Workshops will be conducted using in-person and/or hybrid formats to validate key elements of the proposed framework.

This collaborative approach is intended to ensure that the resulting RPL framework reflects national realities, incorporates stakeholder expertise and develops sufficient ownership to support implementation and endorsement.

7. Finalisation and Government Endorsement Support

After consultation, the consultant will incorporate relevant stakeholder feedback into the final framework.

The consultant will also support the preparation of documentation suitable for endorsement and provide technical input for high-level validation or endorsement meetings.

Consequently, the assignment covers the development process from policy analysis and system design through stakeholder consultation and final preparation for potential government endorsement.

Expected Deliverables

The consultant or consultancy firm will be responsible for producing a substantial set of deliverables.

These include:

  1. Inception Report covering the methodology, workplan and stakeholder engagement plan.
  2. Draft National RPL Policy Framework.
  3. Institutional Architecture and Governance Model.
  4. Assessment and Certification Framework.
  5. Quality Assurance Framework.
  6. RPL Implementation Guidelines / Operational Manual.
  7. Consultation Reports summarising stakeholder contributions and inputs.
  8. Final National RPL Policy Framework, prepared in an endorsement-ready format.

These deliverables demonstrate that the assignment requires expertise spanning policy development, technical design, institutional analysis, stakeholder engagement and practical implementation planning.

Duration of the Consultancy

The consultancy will run from contract signature until 31 March 2027.

Rather than being completed as a single continuous exercise, the work is expected to be organised around phased milestones aligned with stakeholder consultation and validation processes.

The assignment has an estimated level of effort of up to 42 working days, distributed throughout the contract period.

Those working days are intended to cover major deliverables, consultation activities and reporting responsibilities.

Travel, Workshops and Operational Support

Additional operational budget is allocated for workshops, consultations and stakeholder engagement.

Approved consultant travel costs to Sudan, where travel is required and approved, will be handled separately through the operational provision.

Importantly, travel to Sudan is subject to security assessments.

The methodology also anticipates hybrid engagement arrangements combining remote and in-person consultations, reflecting the prevailing security context.

Methodology Expected from the Consultant

The successful consultant or firm is expected to use a methodology appropriate for complex policy and institutional reform.

The British Council specifically expects:

  • A co-creation and participatory approach;
  • A systems approach linking policy, institutions and implementation;
  • Use of international best practices, including relevant ILO and UNESCO approaches and comparative RPL models; and
  • Hybrid engagement modalities, incorporating remote and in-person consultation where appropriate.

Applicants preparing their technical proposals should therefore pay close attention to these methodological expectations.

The proposal should demonstrate not only what the applicant intends to deliver but also how the consultant or team will engage stakeholders, translate international experience into the Sudanese context and develop an implementable national framework.

Reporting and Management Arrangements

The selected consultant or consultancy firm will report to the Youth Skills Programme Manager, British Council Sudan.

Technical coordination will also be maintained with relevant government stakeholders.

The British Council will be responsible for overall contract management and logistical support associated with consultations.

This arrangement means the consultant will need to operate effectively across technical, governmental and programme-management environments.

Required Expertise and Experience

Applicants should demonstrate strong and directly relevant expertise.

The British Council requires proven experience in designing and implementing Recognition of Prior Learning systems or frameworks.

Applicants should also demonstrate strong expertise in:

  • Technical and Vocational Education and Training systems reform;
  • Qualifications frameworks;
  • Skills recognition;
  • Non-formal education systems; and
  • Related policy and institutional development.

Experience working in fragile or conflict-affected contexts is another important requirement.

Applicants should be capable of facilitating complex multi-stakeholder policy processes, given the significant consultation and co-creation responsibilities involved in the assignment.

Familiarity with ILO, UNESCO or other international RPL standards is described as highly desirable.

Additional Considerations for Consultancy Firms

Consultancy firms interested in applying should consider the multidisciplinary nature of the assignment.

For firms, a multidisciplinary team covering policy, assessment and institutional design is preferred.

A strong team proposal should therefore demonstrate how the combined expertise of key personnel addresses the different technical components of the assignment.

Application Requirements

Interested individual consultants and consultancy firms are expected to submit several important documents.

Applicants should prepare:

  1. Technical Proposal – explaining the proposed methodology and approach for undertaking the assignment.
  2. Financial Proposal – providing the financial proposal for delivering the consultancy.
  3. Relevant Experience and References – demonstrating previous experience related to the requirements of the assignment.
  4. CV(s) of Key Personnel – outlining the qualifications and professional experience of the consultant or proposed team members.

The vacancy notice particularly emphasises that applicants should attach the technical proposal for developing the RPL Policy Framework together with their CV.

Applicants should therefore carefully review the Terms of Reference and ensure their technical proposal addresses the assignment’s expected methodology, scope, stakeholder engagement requirements, deliverables and implementation considerations.

APPLY NOW

Ethical Requirements

The selected consultant or consultancy firm must comply with important ethical principles throughout the assignment.

These include adherence to:

  • Do no harm principles; and
  • Data protection and confidentiality standards.

These requirements are especially significant considering the sensitive operating environment and the range of government, civil society, education-sector and development stakeholders expected to participate in the process.

British Council RPL Consultant Application Deadline

The closing date for applications is 26 August 2026.

Applicants should ensure that all required documents are prepared and submitted through the British Council recruitment system before the closing date.

Application Deadline: 26 August 2026

Because the application requires more than a CV, prospective applicants should allow sufficient time to prepare a strong technical proposal, financial proposal, evidence of relevant experience, references and CVs for relevant personnel.

Important Points Applicants Should Remember

Before applying for the British Council International Consultant – Recognition of Prior Learning opportunity, prospective applicants should take note of the following:

  • The consultancy focuses on developing a National Recognition of Prior Learning Policy Framework for Sudan.
  • The assignment requires substantial expertise in RPL systems and frameworks.
  • Strong knowledge of TVET reform, qualifications frameworks, skills recognition and non-formal education is required.
  • Experience in fragile or conflict-affected environments is expected.
  • Applicants must be able to facilitate multi-stakeholder policy processes.
  • Familiarity with ILO, UNESCO or international RPL standards is highly desirable.
  • Consultancy firms preferably should propose multidisciplinary expertise covering policy, assessment and institutional design.
  • The work involves policy development as well as practical implementation guidance.
  • Stakeholder engagement and co-creation are central components of the assignment.
  • The contract is expected to continue until 31 March 2027.
  • The estimated level of effort is up to 42 working days across the contract period.
  • Engagement may involve both remote and in-person activities.
  • Travel to Sudan, where approved, is subject to security assessments.
  • Applicants must submit a technical proposal.
  • A financial proposal is required.
  • Relevant experience and references must be provided.
  • CVs of key personnel must be submitted.
  • The application deadline is 26 August 2026.

Conclusion

The British Council International Consultant – Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) opportunity in Sudan provides experienced education, TVET, qualifications and policy specialists with an opportunity to contribute to an important national skills-system initiative.

At the centre of the consultancy is the challenge of developing a Recognition of Prior Learning system capable of acknowledging competencies acquired through non-formal and informal pathways and connecting those competencies more effectively with recognised qualifications, education and employment opportunities.

The assignment is particularly significant within Sudan’s current context, where conflict, displacement, disrupted education and the dominance of informal economic activity have increased the importance of flexible and inclusive approaches to skills recognition.

The successful consultant or consultancy firm will be expected to move beyond producing a high-level policy document. The work encompasses policy and legal considerations, institutional architecture, governance, competency assessment, certification, quality assurance, implementation guidance, stakeholder co-creation and support for final validation and endorsement.

Professionals and consultancy firms with substantial experience in RPL systems, TVET reform, qualifications frameworks, non-formal education and multi-stakeholder policy development should carefully review the requirements and prepare comprehensive technical and financial proposals.

item.content:encoded:
RMIT University is inviting applications for an exciting Research Fellow in Technology Adoption & Social Change position based in Melbourne, Australia. This four-year, full-time research appointment offers an opportunity for an appropriately qualified social sciences researcher to contribute to multidisciplinary research examining how people, workplaces and communities interact with emerging sensing technologies, artificial intelligence and complex data environments.

The successful applicant will join the Technology Adoption and Social Change (TASC) program within the ARC Industrial Transformation Research Hub for Intelligent Contaminant-Sensing in Complex Environments (IC-SensE). The position brings together social science, technology, artificial intelligence, industry collaboration and human-centred research, making it particularly relevant to researchers interested in the societal implications of emerging technologies.

Based primarily at RMIT University’s Melbourne CBD campus, the Research Fellow will conduct and contribute to high-quality research exploring consumer and workforce adoption of sensor technologies. The researcher will work alongside multidisciplinary academics and industry partners while investigating issues including socially responsible technology design, user experience, data security, trustworthy representation of data and AI-enabled workplace practices.

Applications for the RMIT University Research Fellow position close on 15 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m.

About the RMIT University Research Fellow Position

The Research Fellow, Technology Adoption & Social Change position is a full-time, fixed-term appointment for four years.

The successful candidate will be situated within RMIT University’s School of Global, Urban and Social Studies, which forms part of the University’s College of Design and Social Context. The Research Fellow will also have an affiliation with RMIT’s Centre for Human-AI Information Environments.

This institutional setting provides an interdisciplinary environment in which the successful researcher can contribute social science expertise to research involving technological innovation, artificial intelligence, sensing systems, workplaces, consumers and society.

Key employment details include:

  • Position: Research Fellow, Technology Adoption & Social Change
  • Institution: RMIT University
  • Program: Technology Adoption and Social Change (TASC)
  • Research Hub: ARC Industrial Transformation Research Hub for Intelligent Contaminant-Sensing in Complex Environments (IC-SensE)
  • Location: Melbourne, Victoria, Australia
  • Primary campus: Melbourne CBD campus
  • Employment type: Full-time
  • Contract: Fixed term for four years
  • Academic classification: Academic Level B
  • Superannuation: 17%
  • Working arrangements: Flexible working arrangements are available
  • Application deadline: 15 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m.
  • RMIT job requisition number: JR49996

Although the role is based at RMIT’s Melbourne CBD campus, the successful candidate may be required to work at or be based at other RMIT University campuses when necessary.

What Is the Technology Adoption and Social Change Program?

The Technology Adoption and Social Change (TASC) program is part of the broader IC-SensE research initiative.

TASC investigates how consumers and workers adopt and experience sensing technologies, with particular attention to the human and social dimensions of technological change.

Rather than examining sensing technologies exclusively from an engineering or technical perspective, the program uses human-centred social research methodologies to understand what happens when technologies enter workplaces, industries and people’s everyday experiences.

The program therefore addresses questions surrounding the relationship between technological innovation and society.

Areas examined through the program include:

  • Consumer adoption of sensor technologies
  • Workforce adoption of emerging technologies
  • Human-centred technology implementation
  • Socially responsible technology design
  • User experiences of sensing technologies
  • Data security
  • Trust in technology and data
  • Trustworthy representation of data
  • Artificial intelligence in workplaces
  • AI-enabled work practices
  • Social implications of technological adoption
  • Interactions between technology, workers, consumers and organisations

The Research Fellow will play an important role in developing research that can help researchers, industries and other stakeholders understand these issues.

About the ARC Research Hub IC-SensE

The ARC Industrial Transformation Research Hub for Intelligent Contaminant-Sensing in Complex Environments (IC-SensE) is a multidisciplinary research initiative focused on developing human-focused sensing technologies integrated with artificial intelligence.

IC-SensE received $4.75 million in funding through the 2025 round of the ARC Industrial Transformation Research Program scheme.

The Hub focuses on technologies capable of supporting the real-time assessment of contaminants and helping predict potential hazards before they occur.

This means its work extends beyond simply detecting contaminants. By combining sensing technologies with artificial intelligence, researchers aim to create systems capable of generating timely information that could help anticipate and manage potential risks.

At the same time, IC-SensE recognises that successful technology development and deployment involves more than technical capability.

New sensing and AI technologies ultimately interact with people, workplaces, organisations and communities. Questions surrounding trust, adoption, usability, security, ethics, social responsibility and workplace practices can therefore become central to whether new technologies achieve meaningful impact.

This is where the TASC program and the Research Fellow position become particularly important.

Learn more at https://icsensehub.org.au/

A Multidisciplinary Research Environment

IC-SensE brings together researchers from Australian and international universities alongside industry leaders.

Participating researchers represent fields including:

  • Engineering
  • Computer science
  • Health
  • Built environment
  • Social science

Industry engagement spans areas such as:

  • Health and medical devices
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Environmental industries
  • Energy
  • Software development
  • Defence

Within this broad interdisciplinary environment, the TASC team contributes social science expertise and examines the human and social implications of sensing technologies across different contexts.

The team is led by social scientists who collaborate across disciplinary boundaries to understand workplace and consumer experiences of technology adoption.

For the successful Research Fellow, this creates an opportunity to conduct social science research while collaborating with experts working across technology, AI, engineering, health and other disciplines.

What Will the Research Fellow Do?

The successful candidate will lead and contribute to high-quality research within the Technology Adoption and Social Change program.

An important component of the position involves examining the adoption of sensor technologies from a human-centred perspective using social research methodologies.

The Research Fellow will work collaboratively with researchers from different academic disciplines as well as industry partners.

Research areas may include:

  1. Socially Responsible Design

    The researcher may examine how sensing technologies can be designed and introduced in ways that recognise social needs, responsibilities and consequences.

  2. User Experience

    Understanding how workers, consumers and other users interact with technologies is central to successful adoption. The Research Fellow may investigate people’s experiences, expectations, concerns and responses when engaging with sensing systems.

  3. Data Security

    Sensor technologies can generate significant amounts of information. Research within the program can therefore involve questions surrounding the security and responsible management of data.

  4. Trustworthy Data Representation

    Producing data is only one part of a technological system. People also need to understand and appropriately interpret information generated by technologies. The Research Fellow will contribute to research concerning trustworthy ways of representing and communicating data.

  5. AI-Enabled Work Practices

    As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into workplaces, researchers need to understand how it affects workers, organisations and established professional practices.

    The TASC program provides an environment for examining these changing relationships between people, AI and work.

Research Outputs and Academic Responsibilities

The Research Fellow will be expected to contribute to RMIT’s broader research performance.

The successful candidate will develop productive research networks and generate high-quality research outputs.

Responsibilities are expected to include activities such as:

  • Conducting high-quality academic research
  • Developing new research initiatives
  • Producing scholarly research outputs
  • Contributing to publications
  • Building productive academic and professional research networks
  • Working with multidisciplinary researchers
  • Collaborating with industry partners
  • Applying for competitive research funding
  • Managing research projects
  • Translating research findings for different audiences
  • Contributing to policy and practice
  • Engaging government, industry and community stakeholders
  • Supporting research with economic, environmental and societal relevance
  • Potentially engaging, collaborating with and/or supervising higher degree by research candidates

The position therefore combines independent research with teamwork, stakeholder engagement, research translation and academic collaboration.

Research With Practical Economic, Environmental and Societal Impact

One of the notable aspects of the position is its emphasis on translating academic findings into accessible and actionable outcomes.

The successful applicant will not only be expected to produce academic research but also to consider how research findings can generate wider value.

IC-SensE aims to ensure that its projects benefit participating universities and industry partners while creating broader impacts for:

  • The economy
  • The environment
  • Society

This makes research translation an important element of the Research Fellow’s responsibilities.

Applicants with experience communicating research beyond traditional academic audiences may therefore find this aspect of the role particularly relevant.

Mandatory Academic Qualification

RMIT University identifies one mandatory academic requirement for the position:

Applicants must hold a PhD or equivalent qualification in a relevant social sciences research field.

Candidates who do not meet this mandatory requirement should carefully review the official position description before applying.

Because the program examines technological adoption from a social and human-centred perspective, the position requires strong social science research expertise rather than solely technical expertise in sensing technologies or artificial intelligence.

Research Experience and Track Record Required

Successful applicants should demonstrate an emerging track record and recognition for producing quality research outputs capable of contributing to RMIT’s existing high-performing research teams.

Evidence may include:

  • Academic publications
  • Development of new research initiatives
  • Participation in competitive research funding
  • Contributions to policy
  • Contributions to professional or organisational practice
  • Other evidence demonstrating research quality and impact

The wording of the position indicates that RMIT is looking for someone capable of contributing meaningfully to established research teams while continuing to develop their own research profile.

Qualitative and Social Research Methodology Experience

Applicants should have demonstrated experience designing and conducting qualitative research.

The role particularly emphasises interdisciplinarity and social sciences methodologies aligned with the work of the IC-SensE Hub.

Relevant methodological experience may include:

  • Qualitative research
  • Participatory research methods
  • Mixed-methods research
  • Other relevant social research methodologies

Applicants should clearly demonstrate their methodological capabilities when addressing the Key Selection Criteria.

Where possible, candidates should provide concrete examples of previous research projects, their methodological responsibilities, the research questions addressed and the resulting outputs or impact.

Industry, Government and Community Engagement

The position is not limited to university-based research.

RMIT is seeking candidates with experience engaging with industry, government or community stakeholders through collaborative research projects and/or research translation activities.

Applicants should therefore consider highlighting previous experience involving:

  • Industry research partnerships
  • Government collaboration
  • Community-based research
  • Research translation
  • Stakeholder consultation
  • Collaborative research projects
  • Policy engagement
  • Knowledge exchange
  • Projects designed to create societal impact

The ability to communicate effectively with people outside the candidate’s immediate academic discipline is particularly valuable in a multidisciplinary research hub.

Independent and Collaborative Working Skills

The successful applicant must be capable of working independently while also contributing effectively to teams.

The position requires someone who can:

  • Manage independent research responsibilities
  • Lead teams when required
  • Collaborate across academic disciplines
  • Build relationships with researchers
  • Engage external stakeholders
  • Work constructively within multidisciplinary project environments

This balance is particularly important because IC-SensE incorporates researchers from several academic fields and collaborates with multiple industry sectors.

Competitive Research Funding Experience

Candidates should have experience applying for competitive research funding and successfully managing research projects.

Applicants preparing their application may therefore want to provide specific evidence of involvement in:

  • Grant applications
  • Research funding proposals
  • Funded research projects
  • Project planning
  • Research project management
  • Budget or resource management, where relevant
  • Delivery of project milestones
  • Reporting and research outputs

Applicants do not necessarily need to restrict examples to projects for which they were the sole lead researcher. Where appropriate, they can clearly explain their individual contribution to collaborative applications and funded research projects.

Communication and Interpersonal Skills

Excellent communication and interpersonal abilities are essential for the Research Fellow position.

RMIT specifically seeks candidates capable of confidently and effectively working with:

  • Academic colleagues
  • Project team leaders
  • Industry stakeholders
  • Community stakeholders
  • Government stakeholders
  • Higher degree by research candidates

Strong scholarly communication practices are also required.

The successful applicant may be expected to communicate complex research findings to audiences with different levels of technical and academic expertise.

Opportunity to Work at the Intersection of Social Science and Artificial Intelligence

One particularly interesting feature of this position is the opportunity to contribute to research at the intersection of social science, sensing technology and artificial intelligence.

The Research Fellow will be affiliated with RMIT’s Centre for Human-AI Information Environments, in addition to being based within the School of Global, Urban and Social Studies.

This provides an environment for examining not only whether technologies function effectively, but how people understand, trust, adopt and experience them.

For researchers interested in the social dimensions of AI, human-centred technology, responsible innovation and changing workplace practices, the position offers a substantial four-year research appointment within an interdisciplinary program.

Salary, Superannuation and Working Arrangements

The Research Fellow position is classified at Academic Level B.

In addition to the applicable Academic Level B salary, the successful candidate will receive 17% superannuation.

RMIT also states that flexible working arrangements are available.

Applicants should consult the official RMIT vacancy and associated position description for complete employment conditions and the applicable salary information.

Location: Melbourne, Australia

The position is primarily based at RMIT University’s Melbourne CBD campus in Melbourne, Victoria, Australia.

However, RMIT notes that the successful candidate may be required to work and/or be based at other University campuses.

Applicants considering relocation should independently investigate practical matters such as Australian work rights, immigration requirements, accommodation and relocation costs where relevant. The supplied vacancy information does not state that visa sponsorship or relocation assistance is provided, so applicants should not assume that either benefit is available unless confirmed directly by RMIT.

Pre-Employment Checks

Appointment to the position is subject to required background screening.

RMIT states that appointment is subject to passing:

  • A Working with Children Check
  • A National Police Check

From 1 January 2026, RMIT also considers gender-based violence risk factors as part of its recruitment processes.

Applicants are required to complete a gender-based violence declaration in accordance with the National Higher Education Code to Prevent and Respond to Gender-based Violence.

Preferred candidates will also be required to undertake relevant pre-employment background checks.

RMIT University’s Equal Opportunity Commitment

RMIT describes itself as an equal opportunity employer and a child-safe organisation.

The University states that it is committed to attracting, retaining and developing people regardless of:

  • Gender identity
  • Ethnicity
  • Sexual orientation
  • Disability
  • Age

Applications are encouraged from all sectors of the community, with RMIT particularly encouraging applications from the Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander community.

RMIT also actively supports and encourages people with disability to apply and provides support for adjustments throughout recruitment, selection and employment.

Candidates requiring adjustments during the recruitment process can contact RMIT’s talent support service using the contact information provided on the official vacancy.

RMIT is also a Circle Back Initiative Employer, meaning it commits to responding to every applicant.

How to Apply for the RMIT Research Fellow Position

Applications must be submitted through the official RMIT University recruitment system.

Candidates are instructed to submit:

  1. Curriculum Vitae (CV)
  2. Covering letter addressing the Key Selection Criteria

Applicants should pay particular attention to the requirement to address the Key Selection Criteria.

Rather than submitting a generic cover letter, candidates should use their application to demonstrate how their qualifications, research experience, methodological expertise, funding experience, stakeholder engagement and communication abilities correspond to the requirements of the position.

Where appropriate, applicants can support their claims with specific examples from previous research projects.

APPLY NOW

What Should Applicants Highlight in Their Cover Letter?

Because RMIT specifically requests a covering letter addressing the Key Selection Criteria, candidates should ensure their application provides clear evidence of their suitability.

Depending on their experience, applicants may want to address:

  • Their PhD or equivalent qualification in a relevant social sciences field
  • Their research specialisation
  • Their publication record
  • Their experience developing new research initiatives
  • Their qualitative research expertise
  • Their experience with participatory and/or mixed-methods research
  • Their ability to work across disciplines
  • Their experience working with industry, government or community stakeholders
  • Their involvement in research translation
  • Their experience applying for competitive research funding
  • Their research project management experience
  • Their ability to work independently
  • Their experience leading or contributing to research teams
  • Their scholarly communication skills
  • Their ability to communicate with non-academic stakeholders
  • Their experience engaging with or supervising higher degree research candidates, where applicable
  • Examples of research contributing to policy, practice or societal impact

Applicants should ensure that all statements are accurate and supported by their actual experience.

Application Deadline

The deadline for applications is:

15 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m.

Prospective candidates should aim to submit their application well before the deadline to allow sufficient time to complete the online application, upload the required documents and address the Key Selection Criteria thoroughly.

Applications should be made through RMIT University’s official careers portal.

Further Information and Contact

Candidates who require further information about the position can contact:

Lisa Given
Enabling Impact Platform Director, Social Change
RMIT University
Email: lisa.given2@rmit.edu.au

Applicants should also review the official Research Fellow Position Description available through the RMIT University vacancy page before applying.

Additional information about the IC-SensE Research Hub is available through the Hub’s official website.

Why This Research Position Is Significant

The RMIT University Research Fellow in Technology Adoption & Social Change position provides an opportunity to investigate one of the increasingly important questions surrounding technological innovation: how emerging technologies interact with people and society.

Sensor systems and artificial intelligence can offer substantial technical capabilities, but successful adoption depends on more than technological performance.

Workers and consumers need to understand technologies. Organisations must consider responsible implementation. Data must be managed and represented appropriately. Users need to determine whether systems are trustworthy. Workplaces must adapt to new AI-enabled practices.

These human and social questions sit at the heart of the TASC program.

For an appropriately qualified social sciences researcher, the four-year appointment offers an opportunity to investigate these issues while participating in a multidisciplinary ARC-funded research environment connecting universities and industry.

Conclusion

Applications are now invited for the RMIT University Research Fellow, Technology Adoption & Social Change, ARC Research Hub IC-SensE position in Melbourne, Australia.

The successful candidate will join a multidisciplinary research environment focused on the intersection of sensing technology, artificial intelligence, social research and human-centred technology adoption. Working within the Technology Adoption and Social Change program, the Research Fellow will contribute to research concerning socially responsible design, user experience, data security, trustworthy data representation, AI-enabled work practices and the broader societal implications of emerging sensing technologies.

Applicants must hold a PhD or equivalent in a relevant social sciences research field and should demonstrate strong qualitative and social research capabilities, an emerging record of quality research outputs, experience with research funding and project management, stakeholder engagement skills and the ability to work effectively across disciplinary boundaries.

The appointment is full-time and fixed term for four years, classified at Academic Level B, with 17% superannuation and flexible working arrangements. The position is primarily based at RMIT University’s Melbourne CBD campus.

Interested researchers should prepare a CV and a carefully written covering letter addressing the Key Selection Criteria and submit their application through RMIT University’s official recruitment portal.

Application Deadline: 15 September 2026 at 11:59 p.m.

Candidates are strongly advised to read the complete position description and official vacancy information before submitting their application.

Visit the OFY website for more Job Opportunities.

item.content:encoded:
The University of British Columbia (UBC) Four Year Doctoral Fellowship (4YF) is a major doctoral funding opportunity designed to support outstanding students undertaking advanced research at one of Canada’s leading universities. The fellowship provides substantial financial support to eligible doctoral students, including international students, Canadian citizens, and permanent residents.

Effective September 2026 onward, recipients of the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship can receive a $24,000 annual stipend plus full tuition coverage per year for up to four years of their doctoral studies.

The Four Year Doctoral Fellowship program is intended to help UBC attract and retain exceptional doctoral researchers while giving recipients stable base-level financial support for their studies and research.

One particularly important feature of the 4YF is its application process. Students do not normally submit a separate application specifically for the fellowship. Instead, PhD, DMA, and MDPhD applicants who are offered admission to UBC are automatically considered for 4YF funding.

For prospective doctoral students searching for UBC scholarships for international students, fully funded PhD opportunities in Canada, doctoral scholarships in Canada, UBC PhD funding, or Canadian scholarships for international doctoral students, the Four Year Doctoral Fellowship is an important funding opportunity to consider.

UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship 2026 Overview

Here are the major details prospective applicants should know:

  • Host institution: The University of British Columbia (UBC)
  • Campus: Vancouver Campus, Canada
  • Program: Four Year Doctoral Fellowship (4YF)
  • Degree level: Doctoral
  • Eligible doctoral programs: PhD, DMA, and MDPhD
  • Annual stipend: $24,000
  • Tuition: Full tuition coverage
  • Maximum funding period: Up to four years
  • Citizenship eligibility: Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and international students
  • Selection basis: Academic excellence and recommendation by the graduate program
  • Application method: Apply for admission to an appropriate UBC graduate program
  • Separate 4YF application: Generally not required for incoming applicants
  • Deadline: Set individually by each UBC graduate program
  • New funding level effective: September 2026 onward

What Is the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship?

The Four Year Doctoral Fellowship, commonly referred to as the 4YF, is a funding program established by the University of British Columbia to support high-achieving doctoral students.

Doctoral education can require several years of intensive academic study, original research, laboratory or fieldwork, data collection, academic writing, and dissertation preparation. Stable funding can therefore be an important factor in allowing doctoral researchers to concentrate on their academic work.

Through the 4YF program, UBC provides selected doctoral students with a combination of stipend funding and tuition support.

The university describes the program as a mechanism that allows UBC to continue attracting and supporting outstanding domestic and international doctoral students while providing recipients with stable, base-level funding for their doctoral studies and research.

UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship Value

Beginning September 2026, the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship provides recipients with:

$24,000 Annual Stipend

Successful recipients can receive $24,000 in stipend funding per year.

The stipend provides financial support while recipients undertake their doctoral studies and research.

Full Tuition Coverage

In addition to the $24,000 stipend, the fellowship provides tuition coverage.

This makes the funding package particularly significant because the fellowship addresses both tuition expenses and provides a stipend.

Funding for Up to Four Years

The 4YF can provide funding for up to four years of doctoral study.

However, applicants should understand that four years represents the potential maximum duration rather than a guarantee that every recipient will receive precisely four years of support. UBC states that the duration can be shorter in certain circumstances.

Recipients should consult the official 4YF Guidelines for detailed policies governing the duration and administration of their funding.

Funding is also subject to recipients maintaining satisfactory academic progress.

How Much Could the UBC 4YF Be Worth Over Four Years?

At the stated rate of $24,000 per year, a recipient funded at that stipend level for the full four years could receive up to $96,000 in stipend funding, in addition to applicable tuition coverage.

The calculation is:

$24,000 per year × 4 years = $96,000 in stipend funding

The actual amount and duration received by an individual student can depend on their circumstances, funding period, other scholarships, academic standing, and the rules contained in UBC’s Four Year Doctoral Fellowship Guidelines.

Who Can Apply for the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship?

The UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship is available to both domestic and international doctoral students.

UBC states that Four Year Fellowships may be held by:

  • Canadian students;
  • Canadian permanent residents; and
  • International students.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to international students seeking doctoral funding in Canada.

There is no country-specific restriction stated in the supplied fellowship information. International students from different regions of the world may therefore be considered as long as they satisfy the relevant UBC doctoral admission requirements and other conditions of the program.

Eligible Degree Programs

The fellowship is generally offered to students beginning their first year of full-time study in one of the following types of doctoral programs:

  1. Doctor of Philosophy (PhD)
  2. Doctor of Musical Arts (DMA)
  3. Combined MD/PhD (MDPhD)

While incoming doctoral students are a major focus of the program, UBC states that Four Year Fellowships may also be offered to continuing students.

Therefore, the fellowship is not necessarily restricted exclusively to new doctoral students.

Priority for Incoming Doctoral Students

Each UBC graduate program receives an allocation of Four Year Fellowships.

Graduate programs assess their incoming and continuing doctoral students and select their strongest candidates for the available fellowships.

According to UBC, priority is given to incoming students.

Prospective doctoral candidates with excellent academic records should therefore pay particular attention to the admission requirements and deadlines of their intended graduate program, because applying for admission is also the route through which incoming candidates are considered for 4YF funding.

UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship Eligibility Requirements

Although individual circumstances can vary, the major eligibility considerations include the following.

1. Applicants Should Be Pursuing an Eligible Doctoral Program

The fellowship is generally intended for full-time students in PhD, DMA, or MDPhD programs.

2. Domestic and International Students Are Eligible

The fellowship is not restricted to Canadian citizens.

Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and international students can hold Four Year Fellowships.

3. Academic Excellence Is Essential

UBC states that selection is based on academic excellence, following a recommendation from the student’s graduate program.

This means admission to a doctoral program does not automatically guarantee receipt of the fellowship.

4. Incoming Students Receive Priority

Although continuing students may receive a 4YF, graduate programs give priority to incoming students when selecting recipients.

5. Recipients Must Maintain Satisfactory Academic Progress

Continued funding is subject to satisfactory academic progress.

Students who receive the fellowship should therefore familiarize themselves with the academic and administrative conditions attached to the award.

Selection and Evaluation Criteria

Selection for the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship is based on academic excellence.

Recommendations are made through individual graduate programs.

This means that the relevant graduate program plays an important role in identifying and recommending candidates for the fellowship.

Because the number of fellowships allocated to each graduate program is limited, applicants should understand that simply satisfying UBC’s minimum doctoral admission requirements does not necessarily mean they will receive a Four Year Fellowship.

Graduate programs review eligible students and offer fellowships to their strongest candidates.

How to Apply for the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship

The application process is relatively straightforward for prospective doctoral students because there is generally no separate 4YF application required from incoming applicants.

Step 1: Identify an Appropriate UBC Graduate Program

Prospective students should first identify a PhD, DMA, or MDPhD program at the University of British Columbia that aligns with their academic background and research interests.

Students planning a research degree may also wish to investigate potential faculty supervisors whose research interests correspond with their proposed area of study.

Step 2: Review the Graduate Program’s Admission Requirements

Admission requirements can vary between UBC graduate programs.

Applicants should carefully review the requirements of the particular program they intend to enter, including academic qualifications, supporting documents, research requirements, language requirements where applicable, and any program-specific conditions.

Step 3: Check the Program-Specific Application Deadline

This step is especially important because there is no single university-wide 4YF deadline listed for applicants.

The deadline is set by each UBC graduate program.

Applicants must therefore check the application deadline for their chosen graduate program and ensure their admission application is submitted on time.

Step 4: Apply for Admission to UBC

To be considered for Four Year Fellowship funding, prospective students submit an application for admission to the appropriate UBC graduate program.

Step 5: Automatic Consideration for 4YF Funding

All PhD, DMA, and MDPhD applicants who are offered admission are automatically considered for Four Year Fellowship funding.

This means applicants generally do not need to prepare and submit an additional standalone application for the 4YF itself.

Step 6: Graduate Programs Select Their Strongest Candidates

Each graduate program receives an allocation of Four Year Fellowships and reviews incoming and continuing students.

The programs then offer the fellowships to their strongest candidates, with priority given to incoming students.

For information about admission procedures and requirements visit the Application & Admission page.

APPLY NOW

UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship Deadline

There is no single deadline for the Four Year Doctoral Fellowship.

Deadline: Set by each UBC graduate program.

Prospective applicants should not interpret the absence of a universal deadline as meaning that applications can be submitted at any time.

Instead, applicants must check the admission deadline for the specific doctoral program to which they wish to apply.

Since admission to an eligible graduate program is the route through which incoming students are considered for 4YF funding, missing the relevant graduate admission deadline could also mean missing the opportunity to be considered for the fellowship for that admission cycle.

Applicants should therefore verify the current deadline directly through UBC’s official graduate program and admission pages.

Nomination Process

The nomination process is primarily handled internally by UBC graduate programs rather than by applicants themselves.

Each graduate program receives a certain number of Four Year Fellowships each year.

Programs review both incoming and continuing students and select their strongest students, with incoming students receiving priority.

After selecting a recipient, the graduate program notifies UBC Graduate and Postdoctoral Studies by submitting a signed University Award Recommendation Form.

For administrative purposes, the program uses award number 6456.

UBC states that it is not necessary to list an award amount on the recommendation form.

Recommendation forms should be submitted at least eight weeks before the requested 4YF start date.

This eight-week timeframe concerns the university’s nomination/recommendation process and should not be confused with the student’s graduate admission deadline.

Tri-Agency Award Holders and the 4YF

The Four Year Doctoral Fellowship also interacts with several major Canadian research awards.

Students holding certain Tri-Agency awards automatically become 4YF designates.

These include:

  • Vanier Scholarships;
  • Doctoral Canada Graduate Scholarships (CGSD);
  • Canadian Institutes of Health Research Doctoral Research Awards;
  • Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council Doctoral Postgraduate Scholarships (PGSD); and
  • Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council Doctoral Fellowships.

Doctoral students who receive qualifying Tri-Agency scholarships may be eligible for 4YF tuition coverage.

They can also receive 4YF stipend and tuition support after their external scholarship funding ends, subject to the applicable time limits.

According to the information provided by UBC, this support can continue until four years after the external award start date or until the end of the student’s fifth year in the doctoral program, whichever occurs first.

Other Major External Scholarship Winners

The 4YF can also interact with other major external scholarships.

Recipients of major external scholarships who are selected as 4YF designates may be eligible for tuition coverage through the 4YF.

They may subsequently receive 4YF stipend and tuition support after their external scholarship funding concludes.

For these recipients, funding can continue until four years after the 4YF start date or until the end of their fifth year in the doctoral program, whichever occurs first.

Students receiving external funding should carefully review UBC’s official 4YF Guidelines to understand how their external scholarship interacts with their Four Year Fellowship designation.

Important Funding Requirement for 4YF Holders

Receiving a Four Year Doctoral Fellowship does not necessarily mean students can ignore other external funding opportunities.

UBC requires 4YF holders to apply for other funding in order to maintain their eligibility for 4YF funding.

The requirements differ depending on the student’s status.

Canadian Citizens and Permanent Residents

4YF holders who are Canadian citizens or permanent residents must apply for Tri-Agency funding every year when eligible.

This is an important condition.

UBC states that eligible Canadian citizens or permanent residents who fail to apply for the required Tri-Agency funding will forfeit their remaining 4YF funding.

Recipients should therefore take this requirement seriously and keep track of relevant external scholarship competitions and deadlines.

International Students

International 4YF recipients are not required to apply to the annual Affiliated Fellowship competition, which is held each fall.

However, international recipients are eligible to enter the competition if they choose.

Doing so may provide an opportunity to compete for Affiliated Fellowships carrying higher stipend amounts, including opportunities such as the Killam Doctoral Fellowship.

Can 4YF Funding Be Interrupted?

UBC provides a mechanism through which 4YF payments can be interrupted for certain non-academic reasons.

Examples given by the university include:

  • Relevant work experience; and
  • Paid internships.

UBC provides a 4YF Interruption Form for recipients who need such an interruption and who do not intend to apply for a corresponding professional leave of absence from the university.

Because interruptions can affect fellowship payments and potentially the administration of an award, recipients considering this option should consult UBC’s official rules and relevant graduate program before making arrangements.

Why the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship Is an Important Opportunity

The UBC 4YF stands out because it combines several significant benefits.

Substantial Annual Financial Support

A $24,000 annual stipend provides recipients with a meaningful base level of financial support during their doctoral studies.

Tuition Coverage

The fellowship also provides tuition coverage, reducing one of the major educational costs associated with completing a doctoral degree.

Potential Four-Year Duration

Funding may be available for up to four years, providing a degree of financial stability over a substantial portion of a recipient’s doctoral studies.

International Students Are Eligible

International students can be considered alongside Canadian citizens and permanent residents, making the fellowship relevant to doctoral candidates worldwide.

No Separate Fellowship Application for Incoming Applicants

Eligible PhD, DMA, and MDPhD applicants who receive an offer of admission are automatically considered for 4YF funding.

This reduces the need to complete a separate fellowship application during the initial admission process.

Broad Research Possibilities at UBC

The examples of current and previous award holders provided by UBC illustrate the breadth of research supported through doctoral study at the university.

Research represented among featured fellowship holders includes areas such as:

  • Microbiology and immunology;
  • Interdisciplinary studies;
  • Zoology;
  • Biochemistry and molecular biology;
  • Oceanography;
  • Population and public health;
  • Gender, race, sexuality and social justice;
  • School and applied child psychology;
  • Resources, environment and sustainability; and
  • Cell and developmental biology.

These examples demonstrate that the Four Year Doctoral Fellowship is not confined to one narrow academic discipline.

Important Points Applicants Should Remember

Prospective applicants should keep several important details in mind:

  1. Apply for admission first. Incoming applicants are considered for the 4YF through their application to an eligible UBC doctoral program.
  2. There is no universal deadline. The deadline is determined by each graduate program, so applicants need to check the deadline for their chosen program.
  3. Admission does not guarantee a fellowship. Applicants offered admission are automatically considered, but individual graduate programs select their strongest candidates from the eligible pool.
  4. Academic excellence is central to selection. The fellowship is intended to support outstanding doctoral students.
  5. Incoming students receive priority. Continuing students may receive a fellowship, but UBC states that priority is given to incoming students.
  6. International students are eligible. The program is open to international students as well as Canadian citizens and permanent residents.
  7. Funding can last up to four years. However, the actual funding period can be shorter depending on individual circumstances and the applicable 4YF policies.
  8. Academic progress matters. Fellowship funding remains subject to satisfactory academic progress.
  9. Other funding obligations may apply. In particular, eligible Canadian citizens and permanent residents holding a 4YF must apply annually for Tri-Agency funding to retain their remaining 4YF eligibility.
  10. Recipients should read the official 4YF Guidelines. Detailed rules concerning the administration, duration, interruption, and interaction of 4YF funding with other awards are contained in UBC’s official guidelines.

Frequently Asked Questions About the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship

Is the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship open to international students?

Yes. UBC states that Four Year Fellowships can be held by both domestic and international students.

How much is the UBC 4YF worth?

Effective September 2026 onward, recipients receive $24,000 in stipend funding plus tuition per year, potentially for up to four years.

Does the UBC 4YF cover tuition?

Yes. Tuition coverage is included in the fellowship funding package.

How long does the fellowship last?

Funding may be provided for up to four years, although the duration can be shorter in some circumstances.

Do applicants need to submit a separate 4YF application?

For incoming applicants, generally no. PhD, DMA, and MDPhD applicants who are offered admission are automatically considered for Four Year Fellowship funding.

What is the deadline for the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship?

There is no single fellowship deadline applicable to every applicant. The deadline is set by each UBC graduate program.

Applicants should check the admission deadline of their intended graduate program.

Are continuing doctoral students eligible?

Yes. Although the fellowships are generally offered to students beginning their first year of full-time doctoral studies, UBC states that continuing students may also receive them.

What degrees qualify for the fellowship?

The fellowship is generally associated with full-time PhD, DMA, and MDPhD studies.

Is the scholarship awarded automatically after admission?

No. Applicants offered admission to eligible programs are automatically considered, but this does not mean every admitted student automatically receives funding. Graduate programs select their strongest candidates based on academic excellence and their available fellowship allocations.

How Prospective Applicants Can Strengthen Their Position

Because selection is based on academic excellence and graduate-program recommendation, prospective students should focus on submitting the strongest possible application for admission.

Applicants should carefully demonstrate their academic preparation, research potential, relevant experience, and suitability for their proposed doctoral program wherever these elements are requested as part of the admission process.

For research-focused degrees, identifying appropriate faculty expertise and understanding the research environment of the intended graduate program can also be an important part of preparing a competitive doctoral application.

Applicants should always follow the specific instructions issued by their chosen UBC program because requirements can vary across departments and disciplines.

Final Reminder About the Deadline

The UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship does not have one universal application deadline.

Deadline: Set by each UBC graduate program.

Prospective students should locate their intended PhD, DMA, or MDPhD program on UBC’s official graduate website, confirm its current admission deadline, and submit all required admission materials according to that program’s instructions.

Applicants should avoid relying on deadlines associated with unrelated UBC programs because different graduate programs may operate according to different application schedules.

Conclusion

The University of British Columbia Four Year Doctoral Fellowship (4YF) represents a significant funding opportunity for outstanding students seeking doctoral education in Canada. With $24,000 in annual stipend funding plus tuition coverage for up to four years, the fellowship can provide recipients with substantial financial support while they pursue advanced research at UBC.

Its accessibility to Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and international students makes the program particularly noteworthy for prospective doctoral candidates worldwide. Moreover, eligible PhD, DMA, and MDPhD applicants who are offered admission are automatically considered for the fellowship, meaning there is generally no separate 4YF application for incoming students.

Competition should nevertheless be expected. Fellowships are allocated among UBC graduate programs, and programs select their strongest students based on academic excellence, with priority given to incoming candidates.

Anyone interested in the UBC Four Year Doctoral Fellowship 2026 should begin by identifying an appropriate UBC doctoral program, carefully reviewing its admission requirements, checking its specific application deadline, and preparing a strong application for admission.

Most importantly, prospective applicants should remember that the deadline is determined by each UBC graduate program. Applicants should therefore consult the official University of British Columbia Graduate and Postdoctoral Studies website and their chosen graduate program for the latest admission requirements, deadlines, funding policies, and Four Year Doctoral Fellowship guidelines before applying.

Visit the OFY website for more Fellowship Opportunities.
